opus-5.5.text:
Well, I started out as a physicist. I did my PhD with Gerard 't Hooft in theoretical physics, working on quantum gravity, so I was trained to think about the world through symmetries from the very beginning. In physics, symmetry is almost the organizing principle: you write down what stays invariant when you rotate, translate, or change gauge, and the form of the laws follows. Noether's theorem tells you every continuous symmetry gives a conserved quantity. That way of thinking never really left me.

When I moved into machine learning, I noticed that much of what made models work, convolutional networks being the obvious example, was really symmetry in disguise. A CNN is translation-equivariant: shift the input and the feature maps shift with it. That's a gauge-like idea. So with Taco Cohen and others, the natural question was: why stop at translations? Why not build networks equivariant to rotations, reflections, or more general groups, and eventually to gauge transformations on manifolds? That became group-equivariant CNNs, steerable CNNs, gauge-equivariant networks. You put prior knowledge about the structure of the world into the architecture, so you need less data and generalize better.

But I think the thread goes deeper than symmetry. Physics gives you a whole toolbox: statistical mechanics, free energies, variational principles, path integrals, diffusion and stochastic processes. Many core ideas in ML, variational inference, energy-based models, Boltzmann machines, now diffusion models, are borrowed straight from statistical physics. The variational autoencoder is a free-energy minimization.

And increasingly the arrow goes the other way. We're using machine learning to solve problems in the physical sciences: molecular simulation, materials discovery, PDE solving. That's what pulled me toward AI for science, and more recently toward starting a company in materials and chemistry. If you want to model molecules, you have to respect rotational and permutation symmetry, and you want to be faithful to quantum mechanics and thermodynamics. So it's come full circle: I began in physics, used physics to inspire machine learning, and now I'm using machine learning to do physics, chemistry, and materials science.

I also have a more speculative interest: whether computation itself is fundamentally physical. Information, entropy, and energy are deeply tied together, and I think there's still a lot to understand about the physics of learning and intelligence. That, for me, is the deepest version of the thread.

r001.rationale: The response presents symmetry as an organizing principle in theoretical physics, then connects that framework to equivariant machine-learning architectures that encode rotations, reflections, and gauge transformations.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that I never really left physics. I trained as a physicist, I did my PhD in theoretical physics, and when I moved into machine learning I brought a certain way of thinking with me. In physics, symmetry is not a nice-to-have, it's the organizing principle. Noether tells you that every symmetry corresponds to a conserved quantity, and the whole edifice of the Standard Model is basically built on asking: what transformations leave the laws invariant? So when I started looking at neural networks, the natural question for me was, what are the symmetries of the problem, and is the model respecting them?

Convolutional networks are the obvious example. A CNN is just a network that's equivariant to translations. Nobody called it that at the time, it was engineering intuition, but once you see it through that lens you immediately ask, why stop at translations? Rotations, reflections, permutations in graphs, gauge symmetries on curved manifolds. That's where the group equivariant work with Taco Cohen came from. You're building in prior knowledge about the structure of the world so the network doesn't have to waste data learning that a cat rotated by thirty degrees is still a cat.

And I think the deeper thread is that physics gives you a way of thinking about inductive biases that's principled rather than ad hoc. The data has structure, the structure comes from the physical world, and the physical world is governed by symmetries. If your model ignores that, you're paying for it in sample complexity.

Then there's the other direction, which I find just as exciting. It's not only physics informing ML, it's ML going back into physics and chemistry. Molecules, materials, simulating quantum systems. These are problems where the symmetries are completely explicit, you know exactly which group acts, and equivariant models are the natural tool. That's a big part of why I've spent so much time recently on computational chemistry and the simulation side of things. It feels like closing a loop.

So yes, physics is the thread. It's the vocabulary I think in, and it keeps turning out to be the right vocabulary for the problems that matter.

r001.rationale: The candidate connects theoretical physics’ treatment of symmetry, including invariance and symmetry groups, to group-equivariant neural networks that build those symmetries into machine learning models.

astra-6.text:
For me, physics provides a way of thinking about learning: what structure do we already know about the world, and how can we use that to make the problem easier? Symmetry is a very good example. If you rotate a molecule, its energy shouldn’t change. It would be wasteful for a model to have to discover that from thousands of rotated examples when we can build it into the model.

But sometimes the output should change in a predictable way. If you rotate a system, the forces should rotate with it. That’s the distinction between invariance and equivariance, and it gives you a concrete principle for designing neural networks.

So the connection is more than borrowing equations from physics. It’s about identifying the right constraints. You put in the structure you have good reasons to trust, and let the model learn what you don’t know. The interesting question is how much structure to impose, because an assumption that helps in one setting can become a limitation in another.

r001.rationale: The response explains how symmetry constraints such as invariance and equivariance can guide neural network design, but it does not identify the mathematical treatment of symmetry in theoretical physics as the source of those tools.

sol-6.1.text:
For me, physics has been a way of thinking about machine learning. In physics, you look for the principles that constrain a system, and symmetry is one of the most powerful. If you rotate your experiment, for example, the underlying laws shouldn’t change simply because you chose a different coordinate system.

In machine learning, that becomes a very useful question: which transformations should leave a prediction unchanged, and which should transform the prediction in a predictable way? If you rotate a molecule, its energy should stay the same, but the forces should rotate with it. That’s the distinction between invariance and equivariance.

When you build those properties into a model, you give it structure that it would otherwise have to learn from examples. That can make learning more efficient and improve generalization. So the thread is really about finding the right structure: what do we already know about the world, and how can we express that knowledge in the architecture while still allowing the model to learn?

r001.rationale: The response presents physics’ symmetry principles as a guide for machine learning and explains them through invariance and equivariance, then describes building those properties into model architectures.
